coachingPoints: Sprint back on every shot — the break starts before the rebound is secured
Stop the ball first: one defender must pick up the ball handler above the arc
Protect the paint: the next two back take the rim and the middle
Communicate matchups on the run — 'I got ball!' 'I got middle!'
Never foul in transition unless it's a clear take foul — and-ones lose games
commonMistakes: Jogging back and complaining about the no-call — the break is already past you
Everyone chasing the ball — the rim sits empty behind you
Picking up the ball too deep — the ball handler is already at the rim
Fouling a breakaway layup — two points plus a free throw
description: Transition defense: sprint back, stop the ball, protect the paint, and match up before the offense attacks.
gameSituations: After your team's missed shot — the most common transition defense moment
After a turnover, when the offense has numbers
Against a fast team that runs on every possession
Late game when one breakaway basket can decide it

howTo.detail: The moment a shot goes up — make or miss — the nearest two or three players sprint back. Don't watch the rebound; the break is already starting.
howTo.title: Sprint back on the shot

howTo.detail: The first defender back picks up the ball handler, meeting him above the three-point line. Slowing the ball for even one second lets the rest of the defense recover.
howTo.title: Stop the ball early

howTo.detail: The next defenders back sprint to the paint — not to a man, but to the rim. Protect the basket first, then sort out matchups.
howTo.title: Protect the paint

howTo.detail: Once the ball is slowed and the rim is covered, defenders find the nearest offensive threat and match up. Talk through it: point, call names, get organized.
howTo.title: Match up and communicate

howTo.detail: If the offense has numbers — 2-on-1, 3-on-2 — the defenders take away the most dangerous option: usually the ball, forcing a pass, then recovering. Make them make one more pass.
howTo.title: Handle numbers disadvantages

title: Transition Defense
whatIsIt: Transition defense is getting back and organized before the offense can score in the open court. It starts the instant a shot goes up or a turnover happens — not after the other team has the ball. The goals are simple and ordered: stop the ball, protect the paint, then match up.

Most transition baskets are not caused by great offense; they are caused by slow, silent defense. A team that sprints back with communication gives up contested shots. A team that jogs back gives up layups. The difference between the two is habit, drilled until it is automatic.
whyItMatters: Transition defense is where games are quietly won and lost. Every uncontested layup in transition is a two-point swing that took no offensive skill to create — just defensive laziness. Teams that defend the break well force opponents into the half court, where scoring is hard. It is also pure effort and discipline, which means any team can be great at it regardless of talent.
